why: Matching each string on a mechanical hand toy to the finger it curls helps your child explain how bones, tendons and joints work together.
teaser: Pull one string on a mechanical hand toy, watch a finger curl, then find the bones, tendons and joints doing the same job in your own hand.
title: How a Hand Works
question: How do bones, tendons and joints work together to curl and open a hand?
idea: A hand has 27 bones linked at joints. Muscles, mostly up in the forearm, pull long tendons that work like strings, curling fingers at hinge-like joints. Muscles can only pull, so other tendons on the back of the hand pull the fingers straight again.

curiosity.intro: Start with a toy hand on strings. Then look inside your own: bones, tendons that pull like strings, and joints that bend.
curiosity.carryForward: Pull one string, then ask which part of your own hand does that job.

questions.question: What keeps a finger stiff?
questions.notice: Find the short stiff pieces in each toy finger, and count them.
questions.say: Bones. Each finger has three small bones in a row, and the thumb has two. Counting the wrist and palm, one hand has 27 bones. Bones hold the shape, but they cannot move by themselves.
questions.try: Gently press along one of your fingers and count the hard parts between the bends. Count the stiff pieces on one toy finger too. Do the two numbers match?

questions.question: What pulls a finger closed?
questions.notice: Find the thin string that runs along the palm side of a curled toy finger.
questions.say: In the toy, a string. In your hand, a tendon: a tough cord that joins a muscle to a bone. Muscles in your forearm pull long tendons that reach into each finger, and tough loops along the finger hold them close, like the toy's guides.
questions.try: Draw around your hand on paper to make an outline. Pull one toy string slowly and watch which finger curls. Draw a line from that string to the same finger on your outline. Do the same for every string, one at a time.

questions.question: Does your hand work like the toy?
questions.notice: Watch where the toy finger bends, then watch your own finger bend.
questions.say: Both follow one plan: a pull, a string, and joints that bend. Your finger bends at three joints, mostly one way, like a door hinge. The muscles that curl your fingers sit mostly in your forearm, so you can feel them move there.
questions.try: Curl your pointer finger slowly and count the places it bends. Curl the toy's pointer finger and compare. Rest your other hand on your forearm and wiggle your fingers. What do you feel move?

questions.question: What opens the hand again?
questions.notice: Look at the back of the toy hand for elastic, a spring, or a second string.
questions.say: A muscle can only pull, never push. So a second set of tendons runs along the back of each finger and pulls it straight. Many toys use an elastic cord or a spring instead. Some tendons on the back of your hand are linked, which is why one finger can be hard to lift alone.
questions.try: Let go of a toy string and watch whether the finger springs back. Look for what pulls it open. Then lay your hand flat, fold your middle finger under, and gently try to lift your ring finger.

beats.title: A string pulls
beats.passage: Pull one string, and one toy finger curls toward the palm. The string runs through small loops that keep it close to the finger. Your hand has strings too, called tendons. Muscles up in your forearm pull those tendons, and the tendons pull the finger bones. Tough loops along each finger hold the tendons close, just like the toy's loops.
beats.prompt: What does a tendon do when a forearm muscle pulls it?

foldable.heading: A string pulls
foldable.body: Forearm muscles pull long tendons, like strings. Tendons pull finger bones, and loops keep them close, like the toy's loops.

beats.title: Where fingers bend
beats.passage: The toy finger bends in three places, and so does yours. Those bend points are joints, where two bones meet. Most finger joints work like a hinge on a door, folding mostly one way. The thumb's base joint is different. It lets the thumb swing across the palm to touch each fingertip.
beats.prompt: Why do most finger joints fold only one way?

foldable.heading: Where fingers bend
foldable.body: Joints are where bones meet. Finger joints fold like door hinges. The thumb's base joint lets it swing across the palm.

beats.title: String to finger
beats.passage: They pull each string, one at a time, and draw a line from string to finger. The little one curls a real finger slowly and feels the forearm with the other hand. Something moves under the skin near the wrist. The toy and the hand follow the same plan: a pull, a string, and a joint that bends.
beats.prompt: Why can you feel your forearm move when your fingers curl?

foldable.heading: String to finger
foldable.body: Pull each toy string and match it to a finger. Then curl a real finger and feel the forearm move.

beats.title: Opening again
beats.passage: Let go of a toy string, and something must open the finger again. A muscle can only pull, never push. So your hand has a second set of tendons along the back of each finger, pulling it straight. Toys may use an elastic cord or a second string. Why might one of your fingers be hard to lift by itself?
beats.prompt: What pulls a finger straight again?

foldable.heading: Opening again
foldable.body: Muscles only pull, never push. Tendons on the back of the hand pull fingers straight again. Toys may use elastic.

beats.passage: Little Wonderer set a mechanical hand toy upright on the table, its jointed fingers spread wide and five thin strings trailing from the wrist. Beside the little one, Big Wonderer leaned in, curious about what the toy was trying to copy. A real hand curls, grips, and opens hundreds of times a day, yet no strings show on the outside. The toy is a model, a simpler machine that copies one idea from the real thing. Studying the model can point to what hides under the skin.
beats.prompt: What idea might the toy be copying from a real hand?

beats.passage: Each toy finger is a short row of stiff segments, and a real finger follows the same design with three bones called phalanges. The thumb has only two phalanges, which is one reason it moves so differently. Counting the five palm bones and the eight small wrist bones, one hand holds 27 bones in all. Bones are rigid, so they keep a finger's shape and give muscles something firm to pull against. On their own, though, bones cannot move at all.
beats.prompt: Why do muscles need rigid bones to pull against?

beats.passage: When one string is pulled, a single toy finger curls toward the palm, guided by small loops along the way. A real hand uses the same trick with tendons, tough cords that connect muscles to bones. Most of the muscles that bend the fingers sit up in the forearm, and their long tendons cross the wrist into each finger. Fibrous loops called pulleys hold the tendons close to the bones, much like the toy's loops. Without them, a tendon would pull away from the finger like a bowstring.
beats.prompt: What would happen to a tendon without its pulleys?

beats.passage: Both the toy finger and a real finger bend in three places, and each bend point is a joint where two bones meet. Most finger joints are hinge joints, which fold mostly in one direction, much like a door. The knuckle joints can also tilt side to side, so fingers can spread apart. The base of the thumb is a saddle joint, shaped a bit like a rider's saddle. That shape lets the thumb swing across the palm and touch each fingertip, which makes careful gripping possible.
beats.prompt: How does the shape of a joint decide how it can move?

beats.passage: They pulled each string in turn and drew a line from every string to the finger it curled, building a map of the model. Then the little one curled a real pointer finger slowly while resting the other hand on the forearm. Something slid under the skin near the wrist, a sign of muscles working far from the fingertip. The toy and the hand follow one plan: a pull, a cord, and a joint that bends. The model is simpler, but the idea is the same.
beats.prompt: What evidence shows the finger muscles are far from the fingertip?

beats.passage: When a toy string is released, something must open the finger again, because a muscle can only pull and never push. A real hand solves this with a second set of tendons along the back of each finger, pulled by other forearm muscles. Many toys use an elastic cord or a spring for the same job. Some back-of-hand tendons are linked by small bridges, which may explain why the ring finger is hard to lift alone. That leaves a question worth testing on your own hand.
beats.prompt: Why does a hand need muscles and tendons working in pairs?

poem.title: Who Pulls My Strings?
lines: Little Wonderer pulled on a string, only one,
and a toy finger curled like a cat in the sun.
“Who’s pulling MY fingers?” the little one cried.
“I don’t see a string, and I’ve looked on each side!”
Big Wonderer laughed. “You have strings, it is true.
They’re tendons, tucked under your skin, out of view.
Your muscles sit up in your arm past your wrist,
and they tug, and they tug, till your fingers make fists.”
Inside every finger are three bones in a row
(the thumb has just two, as the toy seemed to know),
with joints in between them that fold like a door —
just one way, not backward. (Please don’t try for more.)
But muscles can’t push, so to open back wide,
there are strings on the back, on the knuckle-y side.
So the little one waved at the toy on the shelf:
“We both work on strings — but I pull them myself!”
